groups.high: The Aarhus Convention distinguishes access to environmental information on request under Article 4 from active collection and dissemination under Article 5. Environmental information includes environmental conditions, relevant activities and measures, and human health, safety, or living conditions insofar as affected by environmental factors. A requester need not demonstrate a personal interest. The duty concerns information held by public authorities within the Convention's scope; it is not a promise that an agency must create every analysis requested. Information should be provided as soon as possible, normally within one month, with a justified extension to two months for volume or complexity and notice to the applicant. Defined refusal grounds exist, including protected confidentiality and public-security interests, interpreted restrictively with the public interest in disclosure considered. Emissions information has particular disclosure protection. Where possible, separate disclosable material from protected portions rather than withholding an entire record. Charges must not exceed a reasonable amount. Refusal should give reasons and review information. Article 9 provides a route to challenge an improperly handled request. Proactive duties support accessible public information and immediate dissemination of information enabling the public to prevent or mitigate harm in an imminent threat. The Convention binds its parties rather than automatically every country worldwide. Its purpose is informed participation and accountability, not unconditional release of every document.
groups.mid: The Aarhus Convention gives two linked rights. Article 4 lets you ask for environmental information. Article 5 says public bodies must collect and share facts too. This can cover air, water, soil, activities, and health or safety affected by the environment. You do not have to prove a personal interest. The request concerns information the public body holds. It is not a right to make it create every new analysis you want. It should reply as soon as possible, normally within one month. A large or complex request may take up to two months. You must be told and given reasons. Some information can be refused under defined rules, such as protected privacy or security. Read these rules narrowly. Consider the public interest in release. Facts on emissions have special protection. If only part is protected, the rest should be shared where possible. Any charge must be reasonable. A refusal should explain why and how to seek review. Article 9 protects a route to challenge a badly handled request. Public bodies should also share useful information without waiting for a request. If there is an imminent threat, share useful facts promptly. These should help people prevent or limit harm. The treaty applies to its parties, not automatically every country. The aim is informed public action, not release of every record without limits.
groups.low: You can ask a public body for environmental information under Article 4 of the Aarhus Convention. You do not need to show a personal interest. It may concern air, water, soil, activities, or effects on health and safety. The body must hold the information. It need not create every new analysis you request. It should reply quickly. Normally this means within one month. A large or complex request can take up to two months, but you should be told why. There are limited grounds for refusal, such as protected privacy or security. Officials must read these narrowly. They must consider the public interest in release. Facts on emissions have special rules in favour of release. If only part of a record is protected, they should share the rest where possible. Charges must be reasonable. A refusal should explain the reason and review rights. Article 9 lets you challenge a request that was not handled properly. Article 5 also says to collect and share facts without waiting for a request. Officials should not always wait for people to ask. If harm is imminent, share useful facts promptly. These can help people prevent or reduce the harm. These duties apply in states that are parties to the Convention, not automatically worldwide. The aim is public knowledge and accountability. It is not a right to see every record without limits.
groups.source_review: UNECE information/justice framework and article mapping checked; full PDF access blocked, so no claim of a complete local-law audit.
groups.notes: Qualified original unconditional provision and global application; preserved on-request/proactive distinction.

groups.high: The UN Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals standardizes hazard criteria and communication. It is implemented through national or regional law rather than being a self-executing worldwide mandate. Jurisdictions adopt different editions and building blocks, so the applicable domestic requirements must be checked. A Safety Data Sheet (SDS), formerly often called an MSDS, communicates composition, health and physical hazards, protective controls, and emergency actions. The GHS format has 16 sections: identification; hazards; composition/ingredients; first aid; firefighting; accidental release; handling/storage; exposure controls/personal protection; physical/chemical properties; stability/reactivity; toxicology; ecology; disposal; transport; regulatory information; and other information including revision details. An SDS and container label serve related but distinct purposes. Labels use suitable product and supplier identification, pictograms, signal words, hazard statements, and precautionary advice. The SDS adds exposure limits, personal protection, incompatible materials, spill control, and other detailed information. Disclosure thresholds, exemptions, languages, and update duties depend on the adopted rules. Do not assume any sheet proves safe use: workers need training, suitable controls, and access to the relevant version. Harmonization improves the consistency of warnings, but it does not eliminate all cross-border legal differences or create automatic legal duties for every state solely by publication of a UN edition.
groups.mid: GHS is the UN system for classifying and labeling chemical hazards. Countries use it through their own laws. It is not one law that automatically binds the whole world. Places may adopt different editions or parts, so check the rules where the chemical is used. A Safety Data Sheet, or SDS, gives detailed safety facts. Older sheets were often called MSDS. The format has 16 sections. Section 1 identifies the product. Sections 2 and 3 give hazards and ingredients. Sections 4–6 deal with first aid, fire, and spills. Sections 7–8 cover handling, storage, exposure controls, and protective kit. Sections 9–11 give properties, stability and reactions, and health effects. Sections 12–15 cover effects on nature, waste, transport, and legal information. Section 16 gives other facts and update details. The label is related but different. It gives names, warning pictures, signal words, hazard statements, and safe-use advice. The sheet adds details such as safe exposure limits, gloves, breathing protection, things to keep apart, and spill steps. Rules on ingredients, exemptions, language, and updates vary. Read the right sheet, get training, and use suitable controls. A sheet alone does not make a chemical safe. GHS makes warnings more consistent without making every country's law identical.
groups.low: GHS is a UN system for chemical hazard warnings. Each place puts it into local law. It is not one law for the whole world. Different places may use different editions or parts. Check the local rules. A Safety Data Sheet is called an SDS. An older name is MSDS. It gives details on the chemical and safe use. It has 16 sections. Section 1 identifies the product. Section 2 gives hazards. Section 3 gives ingredients. Section 4 gives first aid. Section 5 deals with fire. Section 6 deals with spills. Section 7 covers use and storage. Section 8 covers exposure controls and protective kit. Section 9 gives properties. Section 10 covers stability and reactions. Section 11 gives health effects. Section 12 covers effects on nature. Sections 13–15 cover waste, transport, and legal details. Section 16 has other information, including preparation and revision details. The label is not the whole sheet. It gives names, warning pictures, signal words, hazards, and safe-use advice. The sheet adds safe limits, gloves, breathing protection, spill steps, and substances to keep apart. Rules for listing ingredients, exemptions, language, and updates can differ. Use the right sheet and get training. You still need safe controls. A sheet does not make a chemical safe. GHS helps warnings match, but local laws are not all the same.
groups.source_review: UN GHS framework/SDS layout checked; no automatic global legal adoption claimed.
groups.notes: Corrected assertion every state is legally required to adopt GHS by GHS itself.

groups.high: The Aarhus Convention makes participation a procedural right rather than an after-the-fact public-relations exercise. Article 7 addresses environmental plans and programs, applying core requirements from Article 6 on reasonable timeframes, early participation while options remain open, and due account of the outcome. Article 6 governs specified activities and other activities meeting its impact criteria; these scopes should not be conflated. Relevant information must be available and the public must have a genuine opportunity to comment. Due account does not mean every objection must be accepted or the public has a universal veto. Plans and programs require a transparent and fair framework; environmental policies are subject to a more qualified endeavor obligation under Article 7. Article 8 separately concerns preparation of generally applicable rules. Access to information and appropriate review under Article 9 support participation, subject to the relevant scope and standing rules. The Convention entered into force in 2001; the European Community became a party in 2005. It was not implemented by an invented EU Aarhus Protocol adopted in 2001. National and EU measures give practical effect, and the Aarhus Compliance Committee reviews compliance without functioning as an ordinary appeal court that automatically annuls permits. Check the type of decision and applicable procedure, not simply whether officials held one meeting after the outcome was settled.
groups.mid: The Aarhus Convention requires meaningful participation in environmental decisions, not just notice after the result is settled. Article 7 concerns plans and programs relating to the environment. It draws on Article 6 for reasonable timeframes, early input while options remain open, and due account of the outcome. Article 6 itself covers specified activities and other activities within its impact rules. These are related but different scopes. People need relevant information and a real chance to comment. Authorities must consider the outcome, but do not have to accept every objection. Participation is not a general veto. Plans and programs need a transparent, fair framework. Policies have a more qualified duty to endeavor to provide participation under Article 7. Article 8 concerns preparation of general rules. Information access and Article 9 review can support these rights, subject to scope and standing requirements. The Convention entered into force in 2001. The European Community became a party in 2005. There was no EU Aarhus Protocol adopted in 2001 implementing it. National and EU measures put duties into practice. The Compliance Committee checks compliance; it is not an ordinary appeal court automatically cancelling permits. Identify the kind of decision and the relevant procedure. A late meeting after all choices are closed is not enough for effective early participation.
groups.low: People should have a real say in environmental decisions before all choices are closed. The Aarhus Convention protects this. Article 7 covers plans and programs. It uses Article 6 rules on enough time, early input, and taking account of the result. Article 6 covers certain projects and activities under its own rules. The two scopes are not identical. People need useful information and a real chance to comment. Officials must consider what comes from that process. They do not have to accept every objection. It is not a general right to veto a plan. Plans and programs need a fair, open process. For policies, Article 7 has a more qualified duty to try to involve the public. Article 8 deals with general rules. Information rights and Article 9 review can help, within the relevant legal conditions. The treaty took effect in 2001. The European Community joined in 2005. It was not put in place by an EU Aarhus Protocol from 2001. National and EU measures carry out its duties. The Compliance Committee checks compliance. It does not automatically cancel permits like an ordinary appeal court. Check what kind of decision is being made and which process applies. A meeting held only after the result is fixed does not give real early input.
groups.source_review: UNECE Article6/7/8 mapping, Convention status and EU2005 party date checked; no automatic judicial remedy claimed.
groups.notes: Corrected plans/programs Article6 misattribution and invented2001 EU protocol; clarified participation not veto.

groups.high: Article 9 of the Aarhus Convention provides three principal access-to-justice routes. First, an unsatisfactory response to an environmental-information request must be reviewable by a court or another independent impartial body; an expeditious free or inexpensive reconsideration route accompanies court review. Second, members of the public concerned meeting the relevant sufficient-interest or impairment-of-right criteria may challenge substantive or procedural legality of decisions within Article 6, with qualifying environmental NGOs recognized under the Convention's rules. Third, members of the public meeting any lawful national criteria must have administrative or judicial procedures to challenge acts and omissions by public authorities or private persons contrary to environmental law. This is not unrestricted standing for every person to challenge every act anywhere. Procedures must be fair, equitable, timely, and not prohibitively expensive, with adequate effective remedies, including injunctive relief where appropriate. Decisions must be written or recorded; court decisions must be publicly accessible. States must provide public information about review and consider assistance reducing barriers. The text does not establish an automatic second judicial appeal in every case, require exhaustion in all circumstances, or universally reverse the burden of proof. Check the specific route, standing, time limits, interim protection, and costs. Participation and review are linked but distinct; merely holding a consultation does not provide an effective remedy for an unlawful decision.
groups.mid: Article 9 of the Aarhus Convention gives three main routes to justice. One concerns information requests. If the response is unsatisfactory, a court or another independent impartial body must be able to review it. Where court review is used, a quick free or inexpensive review route is also needed. The second route concerns decisions covered by Article 6. The public concerned can challenge their substance or procedure when the relevant interest or rights test is met. Qualifying environmental NGOs have protected status under the Convention's rules. The third route allows challenges to acts or failures by public bodies or private persons that breach environmental law. National standing criteria can apply. This is not a right for anyone to challenge every act anywhere. Review must be fair, equitable, timely, and not prohibitively expensive. Remedies must work, with orders stopping harm where appropriate. Decisions must be written or recorded, and court decisions must be public. States must explain review rights and consider help to reduce barriers. Article 9 does not promise a second court appeal in every case, impose the same internal-review steps everywhere, or reverse every burden of proof. Check the route, who can bring a case, deadlines, urgent orders, and costs. Being allowed to comment is different from having a remedy when a decision is unlawful.
groups.low: Article 9 of the Aarhus Convention helps people challenge environmental wrongs. It gives three main routes. First, you can seek review if a request for information went wrong. A court or another independent, impartial body must be able to check it. Independent means free from control by those being checked. Impartial means fair to both sides. If court review is used, there must also be a quick free or low-cost route. Second, you can challenge decisions covered by Article 6. This can concern what was decided or how. The public concerned must meet the right test of interest or rights. Qualifying environmental NGOs have protected status. Third, public bodies or private people may act, or fail to act, against environmental law. Such acts can face administrative or court review. National rules can limit who may bring a case. Not everyone can challenge every act in every place. Review must be fair and timely. It must not cost so much that people cannot afford it. Remedies must work. An order to stop harm may be needed. Decisions must be written or recorded. Court decisions must be open to the public. States must explain review and consider help with barriers. There is no promise of a second court appeal in every case. There is no one rule for internal review or reversal of all proof rules. Check standing, deadlines, costs and urgent protection. A chance to comment is not a remedy for an unlawful choice.
groups.source_review: UNECE three justice routes and safeguards checked directly.
groups.notes: Corrected invented three pillars, universal standing, higher appeal and mandatory exhaustion claims.

groups.high: Rio Declaration Principle 16 promotes internalization of environmental costs and economic instruments, taking the approach that the polluter should in principle bear pollution costs. Authorities should have due regard to the public interest and avoid distorting international trade and investment. The 1992 Declaration is not itself a treaty imposing automatic identical liability on every polluter worldwide. Binding cleanup, compensation, tax, and enforcement obligations arise through the applicable domestic or international regime. Internalization means that costs of preventing or managing pollution are reflected in the activity rather than automatically shifted to the public. Tools may include pollution charges, permit conditions, liability rules, or other economic incentives, depending on the governing law. Prevention, cleanup, and compensation are related but legally distinct; identifying a responsible party and the recoverable costs requires evidence and the relevant standard. Public-interest qualifications do not automatically exempt a polluter because compliance is expensive, and trade considerations do not mean every difference in environmental standards is unlawful protectionism. A carefully designed regime can encourage cleaner production and fairer allocation of costs while considering affected communities. Principle 13 separately calls for development of liability and compensation law. The practical question is which law applies, who caused the harm, what remedy is available, and how costs are assigned—not whether the declaration itself supplies a universal full-cost damages formula.
groups.mid: A polluter should, in principle, bear the cost of pollution. Principle 16 of the 1992 Rio Declaration sets out this approach. It asks authorities to use economic tools and put environmental costs into the activity's costs. This is internalization. The bill is not just left with the public. The principle also says to consider the public interest and avoid distorting international trade and investment. The Declaration is not a treaty with one penalty for all polluters. Other laws set cleanup duties, compensation, taxes, and charges. A fee, permit, liability claim, or incentive may help. Prevention, cleanup, and compensation are not the same legal claim. You need proof of who caused harm and which costs the law covers. High cost does not automatically excuse the polluter. Different standards in two states are not always unlawful trade barriers. Good rules can help cleaner production and protect communities. Principle 13 also calls for work on liability and compensation law. Check the law, cause, remedy, and how costs are assigned. Principle 16 is not one world damages formula.
groups.low: A polluter should, in principle, pay pollution costs. Principle 16 of the 1992 Rio Declaration gives this approach. It asks authorities to use economic tools. The activity should bear the environmental costs. This is called internalization. The public should not simply be left with the bill. The principle says to consider the public interest too. Avoid distorting international trade and investment. The Declaration is not a treaty with one penalty for all polluters. Other laws set binding duties to clean up, pay compensation or pay taxes and charges. A fee or permit may help. A liability claim or incentive may also help. Prevention, cleanup and compensation are different legal issues. You need proof of who caused harm. You must check which costs the law covers. A high cost does not automatically excuse a polluter. Different standards in two states are not always unlawful trade barriers. Good rules can help cleaner production. They can protect communities too. Principle 13 calls for work on liability and compensation law. Check which law applies and what caused the harm. Check the remedy and who pays. Principle 16 is not one world formula for all damages.
groups.source_review: Rio16 wording and UN implementation analysis checked; soft-law status separated from actual liability regimes.
groups.notes: Corrected full-cost automatic liability and automatic trade-distortion inference.

groups.high: Rio Declaration Principle 15 articulates a precautionary approach applied widely according to states' capabilities. Where serious or irreversible environmental damage is threatened, incomplete scientific certainty is not a reason to delay cost-effective preventive measures. This is a response to credible risk under uncertainty, not permission to ignore evidence or a requirement to prove an activity absolutely risk-free. The text does not universally reverse the legal burden of proof. A specific regulatory regime may allocate evidence or safety-demonstration duties, but those must be identified separately. Relevant steps include identifying the potential harm and its seriousness, evaluating available evidence and uncertainty, considering feasible proportionate preventive options, and monitoring or revising decisions as knowledge improves. Limits on an activity, safer alternatives, monitoring, or other controls may be suitable depending on the circumstances. Prevention is not invariably cheaper than remediation, nor does the principle require a blanket ban on all innovation. Cost-effectiveness and state capabilities form part of its formulation. The 1992 Rio Declaration is not itself a treaty establishing one enforcement mechanism worldwide; binding versions and interpretations can differ under national, regional, or sectoral law. The central lesson is that an identified threat of serious or irreversible harm should not be met with inaction merely because every causal detail is not yet settled.
groups.mid: Principle 15 of the Rio Declaration calls for precaution. A serious or irreversible environmental threat may need action before all the science is settled. Lack of full certainty must not delay cost-effective prevention. States should apply this widely according to their capabilities. It does not mean ignoring evidence or proving that every activity is entirely risk-free. It does not always change the burden of proof. A separate law may require a business to give safety evidence. Check that law. First identify the possible harm and how serious it could be. Assess what is known and what is uncertain. Look for practical steps that fit the risk. Safer options, limits, monitoring, or other controls may help. Review the plan as evidence changes. Prevention is not always cheaper than cleanup. It is not a ban on all new technology. Cost-effectiveness and state capabilities matter. The 1992 Declaration is not a treaty with one world enforcement system. National, regional, or sector laws can set binding rules. The aim is not to wait for perfect proof when a credible threat of serious or irreversible harm calls for sensible action.
groups.low: Principle 15 of the Rio Declaration calls for precaution. A serious or irreversible environmental threat may need action before all the science is settled. Lack of full certainty must not delay cost-effective prevention. States should apply this widely according to their capabilities. It does not mean ignoring facts or proving every activity has no risk. It does not always change the burden of proof. A separate law may require a business to give safety evidence. Check that law. First identify the possible harm and how serious it could be. Assess what is known and what is uncertain. Look for practical steps that fit the risk. Safer options, limits, monitoring, or other controls may help. Review the plan as evidence changes. Prevention is not always cheaper than cleanup. It is not a ban on all new technology. Cost-effectiveness and state capabilities matter. The 1992 Declaration is not a treaty with one world enforcement system. National, regional, or sector laws can set binding rules. The aim is not to wait for perfect proof when a credible threat of serious or irreversible harm calls for sensible action.
groups.source_review: Rio15 serious/irreversible, cost-effectiveness and capabilities qualifications checked.
groups.notes: Removed universal burden reversal, absolute safety proof and invariably cheaper prevention claims.

groups.high: Rio Declaration Principle 17, not Principle 14, calls for environmental impact assessment as a national instrument for proposed activities likely to have significant adverse environmental effects and subject to a competent national authority's decision. Assessment should inform authorization before a project proceeds; it is not merely an audit after construction. The Declaration is not itself a detailed worldwide permitting code. The governing law determines triggers, procedure, public involvement, and decision standards. Common EIA stages include screening whether assessment is required; scoping important issues; collecting baseline information; predicting and evaluating direct, indirect, cumulative, and other relevant effects; considering alternatives and mitigation; preparing and reviewing a report; and monitoring compliance and actual outcomes. The baseline describes current conditions, not necessarily an experimental control group. Mitigation commonly prioritizes avoidance, then reduction and restoration, with compensation for residual effects where appropriate. Public information and participation are important under applicable law and related principles, but the detailed passage sometimes attributed to Rio Principle 14 is not its actual wording. An EIA informs judgment; it does not automatically prove a project safe or require approval if a report is submitted. Identify the likely impact, the responsible authority, alternatives, evidence quality, enforceable conditions, and follow-up rather than treating assessment as paperwork alone.
groups.mid: An EIA checks likely harm before a project is approved. EIA means environmental impact assessment. Principle 17 of the Rio Declaration calls for it. The trigger is a proposed activity likely to have significant adverse effects and needing a decision by a competent national authority. This is not Principle 14. The Declaration is not one world permit law. Local law sets the steps and public role. Screening asks if an EIA is needed. Scoping picks the main issues. Gather facts about the place as it is now. That is the baseline. It is not always a control group in an experiment. Predict the effects and assess their seriousness. Relevant direct, indirect, and combined effects matter. Compare other options. Avoid harm first, then reduce it or restore damage. Compensation may help with harm left over where appropriate. A report is reviewed before the decision. People need information and input under the rules that apply. Later monitoring checks real effects and compliance. A report does not prove safety or promise approval. Check risks, evidence, options, authority, conditions, and follow-up. Guide the choice before work starts, not just describe harm afterward.
groups.low: An EIA checks likely harm before a project is approved. It means environmental impact assessment. Principle 17 of the Rio Declaration calls for it. The proposed activity must be likely to have significant adverse effects. It must also need a decision by a competent national authority. This is not Principle 14. The Declaration is not a full world permit law. Local law sets the steps and public role. Screening asks if an EIA is needed. Scoping picks the main issues. Gather facts about the place as it is now. This is the baseline. It is not always a control group in an experiment. Predict effects and check how serious they may be. Look at direct and indirect effects. Combined effects can matter too. Compare other options. Avoid harm first where possible. Then reduce it or restore damage. Compensation may help with harm left over, where appropriate. A report is reviewed before the decision. People need facts and a chance to give views under the rules that apply. Later monitoring checks real effects and compliance. A report does not prove safety or promise approval. Check risk, evidence, options and who is in charge. Check conditions and follow-up. Use the EIA to guide a choice before work starts, not just describe harm afterwards.
groups.source_review: Rio17 actual trigger checked; EIA stages clearly described as common practice, not verbatim treaty mandates.
groups.notes: Corrected Principle14, fabricated quotation and baseline-as-experimental-control claim.

groups.high: Transboundary environmental harm crosses from activities under one state's jurisdiction or control into another state or areas beyond national jurisdiction. Rio Declaration Principle 2 links sovereign resource rights with responsibility not to cause such damage. Principle 19, not Principle 15, calls for prior timely notification and relevant information where activities may have significant adverse transboundary effects, followed by early good-faith consultation with potentially affected states. Notification must allow meaningful consideration, not merely announce a completed decision. Relevant information can include likely effects, uncertainty, proposed safeguards, alternatives, and emergency arrangements. Consultation seeks cooperation on prevention and risk management; the principle does not automatically give the affected state a veto or an unconditional right to halt the activity or demand compensation. Those questions depend on applicable treaties, general law, and facts. Principle 18 separately addresses immediate notification of emergencies likely to produce sudden harmful effects. The International Law Commission's draft prevention articles are relevant guidance but should not be described as a universally ratified treaty or an automatic reversal of proof. Common but differentiated responsibilities under Principle 7 is a different principle, not the source of the notification rule. The Rio Declaration is not itself a detailed global liability code. Identify the activity, likely significant impact, responsible authorities, applicable instruments, and early consultation process.
groups.mid: Environmental harm can cross a border. It can also reach areas beyond national jurisdiction. This is transboundary harm. Principle 2 of the Rio Declaration links resource rights with a duty not to cause it. Principle 19 calls for prior, timely notice and relevant facts. This applies if an activity may have significant adverse cross-border effects. It calls for early talks in good faith. This is not Principle 15. Notice should leave time for a real response. It must not just announce a fixed choice. Useful facts may cover harm, uncertainty, safeguards, other options, and emergency plans. Talks help states manage risk together. They do not automatically let a neighbor veto or stop a project. They do not automatically give compensation. Other law and facts decide those issues. Principle 18 covers quick notice of emergencies with sudden harmful effects. The International Law Commission's draft prevention articles may help. They are not a treaty binding every state or a rule always reversing proof. Principle 7 deals with shared but different responsibilities. That is another idea. The Declaration is not one world damages code. Check the activity, likely harm, laws, and chance for early talks.
groups.low: Environmental harm can cross a border. It can also reach areas beyond national jurisdiction. This is transboundary harm. Principle 2 of the Rio Declaration links resource rights with a duty not to cause it. Principle 19 calls for prior, timely notice and relevant facts. The trigger is an activity that may have significant adverse cross-border effects. It calls for early talks in good faith. This is not Principle 15. Notice must leave time for a real response. It must not just announce a fixed choice. Share facts about likely harm and what is uncertain. Safeguards, other options and emergency plans may matter too. Talks help states manage risk together. They do not automatically give a neighbour a veto or a right to stop a project. They do not guarantee compensation. Other laws and facts decide that. Principle 18 covers quick notice of emergencies with sudden harmful effects. The International Law Commission's draft prevention articles can help. They are not a treaty binding all states. They do not always reverse proof rules. Principle 7 concerns shared but different responsibilities. That is another idea, not the notice rule. The Declaration is not one world damages code. Check the activity, likely harm, law and chance for early talks.
groups.source_review: Rio2/18/19 and distinction from7/15 checked; no automatic veto/compensation asserted.
groups.notes: Corrected Principle15 attribution, CBDR confusion, automatic veto and burden-shift claims.

groups.high: The Basel Convention controls transboundary movements of hazardous and certain other wastes through prohibitions, prior informed consent, and environmentally sound management. Article 4 bars relevant exports to parties that prohibit import and generally forbids trade with nonparties. Article 11 permits qualifying bilateral, multilateral, or regional arrangements, including with nonparties, only under its environmental safeguards; nonparty trade is not simply an ordinary export subject to due diligence. Disposal exports to the area south of 60° south latitude are prohibited. For permissible movements, the exporting state's competent authority notifies the proposed importing and transit states with required information. Written consent and the Convention's conditions, including confirmation of an appropriate contract for environmentally sound management, must be satisfied before movement. Consent alone does not excuse unsafe treatment. Transit, documentation, transport, and take-back or illegal-traffic duties can also matter. The Ban Amendment and domestic law may impose additional restrictions for relevant parties and waste streams. Recycling is not an automatic exemption: recovery operations can fall within the Convention's disposal framework. Conversely, the Convention does not impose a universal rule favoring final disposal over recovery. Its objectives include minimizing waste generation and unnecessary movement and ensuring safe management. Check waste classification, export and import rules, transit, party status, applicable agreements, receiving-facility capability, and the complete consent process.
groups.mid: The Basel Convention controls hazardous and some other waste sent abroad. Article 4 bans relevant exports if a party has banned imports. It generally bans trade with nonparties too. Article 11 allows certain agreements, including with nonparties, if its environmental safeguards are met. This is not a free pass based just on care or good intentions. Export for disposal south of 60° south latitude is banned. For an allowed shipment, the export authority must notify importing and transit states. It must give required facts. Written consent is needed before movement. Other terms apply too. These include confirmation of a suitable contract for environmentally sound management. This means protecting health and the environment when handling waste. Consent does not make unsafe treatment legal. Check transit, papers, transport, waste-return duties, and illegal-traffic rules. The Ban Amendment or local law may add bans for the parties and waste involved. Recycling does not by itself make a shipment exempt. Recovery can be covered by disposal rules. But final disposal is not always preferred to recovery. The aims are less waste, less needless movement, and safe management. Check waste type, state laws and treaty status, any agreement, the plant, and all consent steps.
groups.low: The Basel Convention controls hazardous and some other waste sent abroad. Article 4 bans relevant exports if a party has banned imports. It generally bans trade with nonparties too. Article 11 allows certain agreements, including with nonparties. Its environmental safeguards must be met. This is not a free pass based only on care or good intentions. Export for disposal south of 60° south latitude is banned. For an allowed shipment, the export authority must notify importing and transit states. It must give the required facts. Written consent is needed before movement. Other terms apply too. There must be confirmation of a suitable contract. It must provide for environmentally sound management. This means handling waste to protect health and the environment. Consent does not make unsafe treatment legal. Check transit rules and papers. Check transport, waste-return duties and illegal-traffic rules. The Ban Amendment may add bans for relevant parties and waste. Local law can add bans too. Calling it recycling does not mean it is exempt. Recovery can fall under disposal rules. But the treaty does not always prefer final disposal over recovery. It aims for less waste and less needless movement. It also aims for safe management. Check waste type, each state's laws and treaty status. Check any agreement and all consent steps. Check that the plant can do the job safely.
groups.source_review: Basel Secretariat overview checked for Article4 prohibitions, Article11 agreements and prior-informed-consent process; specific shipment not assessed.
groups.notes: Corrected false no-nonparty-ban and universal disposal-over-recovery preference.

groups.high: The Nagoya Protocol supplements the Convention on Biological Diversity with an access-and-benefit-sharing framework. Benefits from utilization of genetic resources, including subsequent applications and commercialization, are to be shared fairly and equitably with the qualifying provider on mutually agreed terms. Benefits may be monetary, such as fees or royalties, or nonmonetary, such as research results, training, and technology cooperation. Access generally requires the provider party's prior informed consent under its domestic ABS rules unless it determines otherwise. Written mutually agreed terms, not an invented universal Prior Written Agreement instrument, address use, benefit sharing, changes of intent, third-party use, and dispute arrangements where applicable. Indigenous and local communities' established rights and associated traditional knowledge require attention under domestic law and the relevant Protocol provisions, including consent or approval and involvement where applicable. A user may be a researcher or company, not necessarily a user country signing a state-to-state contract. Check national focal points, competent authorities, permits, and the ABS Clearing-House. Article 18 supports appropriate courts, applicable law, mediation or arbitration, and enforcement of judgments; it does not designate ITLOS as a default final tribunal. Mutual recognition between countries does not automatically remove consent or agreed-term duties. Specialized international ABS instruments may alter scope under Article 4. Sovereign resource rights and conservation goals must not be replaced by a simplistic common-heritage or uniform worldwide contract model.
groups.mid: The Nagoya Protocol covers genetic resources. It deals with access and benefit sharing, or ABS. It supports the Convention on Biological Diversity. A user can be a researcher or company. It need not be a country. Benefits from use, later uses and sale should be shared fairly. They go to the provider covered by the rules. Mutually agreed terms set the basis. Both sides must agree to the deal. Gains can be fees or royalties. They can be research results, training or work on technology together too. Access generally needs prior informed consent under the provider country's ABS law. This means permission before access, based on clear facts. That country can decide otherwise. The agreed terms are a written deal. It can cover use, benefits and a changed purpose. It can cover later users and disputes too. There is no one required extra document called a Prior Written Agreement. Indigenous and local communities may have established rights. They may also hold linked traditional knowledge. This is knowledge they hold and pass down. Local law and the Protocol may require their consent or approval and involvement. Check national focal points for guidance. Check the competent authorities, the offices that handle the rules, and any permits. Use the ABS Clearing-House too. Article 18 covers courts, applicable law and enforcing judgments. It covers mediation or arbitration. These are ways to settle a dispute without an ordinary court trial. ITLOS is not the default final court. Mutual recognition means one country accepts another country's laws. This does not by itself remove consent or agreed terms. Under Article 4, a specific international ABS agreement can change scope. Check which rules apply, not one world contract.
